title: Audits, Assessments & Nonconformities
shortDescription: Internal vs external checks, and what actually happens when something doesn't conform — without inventing classification rules that don't universally apply.
genZNote: Finding a gap isn't the failure. Not fixing it is.

sections.heading: Internal Audit, External Assessment, Surveillance, Reassessment

rows: The organisation's own trained internal auditors
Shorter, periodic checks during the validity period
Full-depth check before the accreditation period ends, to renew it

sections.heading: Handling a Nonconformity
sections.body: Important nuance: exact classification systems (e.g. how 'major' vs 'minor' nonconformities are defined) can vary by accreditation programme and by the specific accrediting body's own procedures — never assume one universal classification applies everywhere. The underlying workflow, however, is consistent.

steps.name: Correction
steps.explanation: The immediate fix to the specific instance found — stops the immediate problem.
steps.purpose: Addresses what happened right now, not why it happened.

steps.name: Root cause analysis
steps.explanation: Investigating WHY the nonconformity occurred at a systemic level.
steps.purpose: Without this step, the same gap will likely recur elsewhere.

steps.name: Corrective action
steps.explanation: A systemic change addressing the root cause, so the same nonconformity doesn't recur.
steps.purpose: This is what actually prevents repeat findings.

steps.name: Effectiveness verification
steps.explanation: Confirming, after enough time has passed, that the corrective action actually worked.
steps.purpose: A corrective action that was never verified is just an assumption.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Audits and assessments (internal, external, surveillance, reassessment) are the checking mechanisms of an accreditation system; when a gap (nonconformity) is found, it moves through correction, root cause analysis, corrective action, and effectiveness verification — with exact classification rules varying by programme.
keyFacts: Internal audit is self-initiated by the organisation; external assessment is performed by the accreditation/certification body.
Surveillance is a shorter periodic check; reassessment is a full-depth renewal check.
Correction fixes the immediate instance; corrective action fixes the systemic root cause.
Major/minor nonconformity classification varies by accreditation programme — it is not a single universal system.
commonConfusion: Correction and corrective action are often used as if they mean the same thing — correction fixes THIS instance; corrective action fixes the SYSTEM so it doesn't happen again.

highYieldFacts: Correction = fix the instance. Corrective action = fix the system.
Effectiveness verification is the final, often-skipped step — confirming the corrective action actually worked.
commonTraps: Assuming a single fixed 'major vs minor' nonconformity classification applies across all accreditation programmes — it varies by programme.
mustRemember: Correction → Root cause analysis → Corrective action → Effectiveness verification.

confusedTerms.distinction: Correction is the immediate fix to the specific nonconformity found. Corrective action is the systemic change addressing the root cause, so the same nonconformity doesn't recur elsewhere.
Internal audit is performed by the organisation's own trained auditors, self-initiated. External assessment is performed by the accreditation or certification body itself.

possibleQuestions: Explain the difference between correction and corrective action with an example.
Why can't nonconformity classification (major/minor) be assumed to be identical across all accreditation programmes?

sources.name: NABL — National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories

questions.prompt: A lab immediately re-runs a failed test to give the correct result to the clinician. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: This fixes the immediate instance — that's a correction. Preventing recurrence system-wide would be corrective action.

questions.prompt: True or False: The classification of nonconformities as 'major' or 'minor' is identical across every accreditation programme.
questions.explanation: Classification systems can vary by accreditation programme and accrediting body — there is no single universal rule.
